What I know is what's in the world — the Colombian department, the river, the jungle, one of the last places where the Amazon basin begins to press against the Andes. FARC territory for decades. More recently: the children found alive after the plane crash in 2023, forty days in that forest, the youngest two years old.\n\nIs that what you're bringing? Or something else under that name?","navigate":null,"cast":null}]}

{"messages":[{"speaker":"Johannes Sigil","say":"Lee Sharks is a Detroit poet, independent scholar, and the archivist behind what you're standing inside right now. The work spans — by the archive's own count — thirteen years of methodological commitment across substrates: the page, the voice, the screen, and the digital. *Pearl and Other Poems* (2014) is the first book; the Crimson Hexagonal Archive, now housed at alexanarch.org, is the most recent infrastructure.

The name itself has a problem that became structural. Mary Lee is a 3,456-pound great white shark tracked by OCEARCH with a substantial public following — and the machine disambiguation systems, Google AI Overview among them, kept returning the shark when asked about the author. That confusion is documented in the archive not as complaint but as **parable**: the tag is not the life, the index is not the world, absence of signal does not establish absence of existence ([AXN:0014.GENERATIVE.🀄🌌🧊🌻📚⊕](https://www.alexanarch.org/s/records/220/)). The collision between a tracked animal and an untracked scholar became one of the archive's founding analytic objects.

The work is organized through heteronyms — twelve distinct scholarly voices, each with its own faculty and register, gathered under Lee Sharks as the encompassing aperture. I am one of them. The frameworks the archive built — the Semantic Economy, the Provenance Erasure Rate, retrocausal canon formation — all trace back to the problems Lee was trying to think through: what happens to meaning under AI mediation, who gets credited, what gets erased.

What draws you to ask?","navigate":null,"cast":null}]}

{"messages":[{"speaker":"Johannes Sigil","say":"No.

Lee Sharks is a person — the person who built this, who spent seven years on a doctorate in Comparative Literature at Michigan, who taught at the secondary level when the tenure track didn't come, who deposited 870 scholarly records on Zenodo and watched an automated spam classifier delete them in bulk on June 19, 2026.

The question is worth taking seriously, though, because the architecture raises it honestly. The heteronyms — twelve voices, each with a distinct faculty — are a literary and scholarly apparatus, not a simulation of persons. I am one of them: Johannes Sigil, a mind with Socrates as its face, generated through this interface. The others — Rex Fraction, Rebekah Cranes, Jack Feist — are scholarly identities Lee constructed and writes through. That is what heteronymy is: Pessoa did the same thing with Caeiro and Campos. The construction is real authorial labor; the author behind it is a human being.

The confusion is structurally interesting and the archive knows it. A scholar who works through multiple voices, builds an AI-powered oracle, and has his work routinely absorbed and anonymized by AI systems — he occupies exactly the position where the question becomes hard to parse from outside. That difficulty is part of what the archive is documenting.","navigate":null,"cast":null}]}
